title: Reverse Linked List
interviewTips: Ask if you must mutate original nodes in-place versus creating new nodes, and whether input can be empty or cyclic.
Trade-off: iterative O(1) space is production-preferred; recursion is elegant but risks stack overflow on long lists, stack-based uses O(n) extra space.
Edge-case tip: always test empty list, single node, two nodes, and ensure original head next is set to null to avoid a cycle.

approaches.name: Approach 1: Stack-Based Reversal
approaches.intuition: Push all nodes onto a stack to reverse their order, then pop them to rebuild links from tail to head. Last-in-first-out naturally gives reversed order.
approaches.theory: Traverse once pushing each node pointer onto a stack. The top is the original tail which becomes new head. Pop one by one linking curr.next to popped node. Finally set last node next to null. This uses extra storage to avoid careful pointer juggling but still runs in linear time.

code.python:
class Solution:
    def reverseList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        stack = []
        curr = head
        while curr:
            stack.append(curr)
            curr = curr.next
        if not stack:
            return None
        new_head = stack.pop()
        curr = new_head
        while stack:
            node = stack.pop()
            curr.next = node
            curr = node
        curr.next = None
        return new_head

timeComplexity.explanation: Each of n nodes is pushed once and popped once, two linear passes.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Stack stores n node pointers in addition to input.

steps: push 1, push 2, push 3, stack top is 3

edgeCases: Empty list returns null without stack access
Single node push then pop returns same node with next set to null
Must set final curr.next to null else original head still points forward and creates cycle

approaches.name: Approach 2: Iterative In-Place Reversal
approaches.intuition: Walk the list once flipping each next pointer to point backward. Keep prev as new head built so far and nxt to not lose the rest of the list.
approaches.theory: Maintain invariant: nodes before curr are already reversed with prev as their head, nodes from curr onward are untouched. For each curr, save nxt=curr.next, redirect curr.next=prev, then advance prev=curr and curr=nxt. When curr becomes null, prev is the new head. Only three pointers are needed.

timeComplexity.explanation: Single pass visits each node once with O(1) work per node.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Only prev, curr, nxt pointers, no extra allocation proportional to n.

edgeCases: Empty list: loop skipped, return null
Single node: one flip to null, returns same node
Two nodes: verifies nxt save prevents losing second half

approaches.name: Approach 3: Recursive Reversal
approaches.intuition: Reverse the suffix starting at head.next, then make that suffix tail point back to head. Let recursion handle all but the first edge.
approaches.theory: Base case: empty or single node is already reversed. Recursive step: newHead=reverse(head.next) is head of reversed suffix. The suffix tail is head.next, so set head.next.next=head to append head at end, then head.next=null to break old link. Unwinding builds full reversal. Call depth equals list length.

timeComplexity.explanation: n recursive calls each doing O(1) pointer rewiring.

spaceComplexity.explanation: Recursion call stack depth n in worst case, plus O(1) extra per frame.

steps: reverse(1) calls reverse(2) calls reverse(3) returns 3

edgeCases: Empty list hits base case and returns null
Single node hits head.next==null and returns itself
Long list may cause stack overflow in languages with limited recursion depth, prefer iterative
